title: The hypertrophy series: volume vs intensity
summary: An introductory hypertrophy series episode defining volume (reps, sets, and how much muscle is worked, producing tonnage) and intensity (relative to your one-rep capacity, rising within a set and with pre-fatigue). He doesn't use RPE or know his 1RM. The key point: volume only builds muscle inside the right intensity window, where the target muscle, not cardio or mechanics, is what fails.

claims.claim: He breaks hypertrophy theory into short ~10-minute episodes, planning a weekly upload and at least 50 episodes.
Volume is the number of reps and sets, and also depends on how much muscle mass is worked, since that drives the energy needed to recover; high volume for legs costs far more than for biceps.
The direct result of volume is tonnage.
Intensity is tied to your body's ability to move a weight once, so you need some idea of your maximal capacity to discuss it.
He doesn't use RPE because he doesn't know his one-rep max, and it has never stopped him from programming with intensity; he won't teach what he doesn't personally know.
Intensity ramps up within a set: on a 12-rep set at 70%, the 12th rep is more intense than the first because you're pre-fatigued.
Pre-fatiguing a muscle in a superset (e.g. push-ups before bench) effectively raises intensity: a 50% bench load can act like 65%.
Volume is incredibly important for hypertrophy but only counts if it falls within the right intensity window; otherwise it's junk volume.
Most people do volume at too low an intensity, so they stop from cardiovascular or mechanical failure instead of muscular failure.
The goal is for the target muscle to be the limiting factor so the set ends because that muscle can't continue; that muscle has reached failure at the right intensity and will grow.
A program must combine both: know what is challenging enough to produce results and how much of that stimulus you need, while keeping it sustainable.
